Every state has its own FWC. These are the official state agencies for this region — registration, boating laws, fishing licenses and state-run launch lists, straight from the source. The state sites carry the official rules.

Florida Fish & Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC)

Florida's FWC — boating laws & safety, the safety-education card, fishing licenses and the state's own boat-ramp finder. One job is NOT FWC's: registration and titling are issued through your county Tax Collector's office, under the FL Dept. of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles — FWC's own regulations page states this.

Register a boat
Vessel Titling & Registrations — FLHSMVTitles and registrations run through your local county Tax Collector's office; a vessel must be registered and numbered within 30 days of purchase.
Boating laws
Boating Regulations — FWCFlorida's boating rules straight from FWC — registration, safety equipment, and who may operate.
Safety card
Boating Safety Education ID Card — FWCAnyone born on or after Jan. 1, 1988 needs this card to operate a motor of 10 hp or more; a NASBLA-approved course from another state or Canada also counts.
Fishing
Licenses & Rules — FWCRecreational fishing licenses and rules; licenses are bought through FWC's GoOutdoorsFlorida portal.
Public launches
Boat Ramps & Access — FWCFWC's own ramp inventory — home of the Florida Boat Ramp Finder.

Daily Report — Wednesday, November 11, 2026

Today's Best Bets

1. Redfish — still the top bet as the bay cools into mid-November. Recent local guide roundups describe the bite as strong, with bigger fish showing more often, on grass flats, mangrove shorelines and oyster bars around Weedon Island, Fort De Soto and Cockroach Bay, plus creek mouths holding bait. Throw live sardines / greenbacks or scaled sardines up under the mangroves, fresh cut bait on the bars, or a gold spoon / weedless soft plastic across the flats — fish the dawn outgoing 5:30–9:40 AM at creek mouths, then the long incoming 9:40 AM–4:36 PM up tight as the flats flood.
2. Spotted Trout — in their reliable fall pattern on deeper grass flats, potholes and sand holes in 3 to 6 feet around Weedon Island, Fort De Soto and the Pinellas flats, especially where bait is present. Guide and shop reports call the bite steady this week on soft-plastic jigs, with live shrimp under a popping cork a reliable producer, and pompano starting to mix in around the same flats. Try a topwater or jig at first light on the falling tide, then slow down over the potholes — best on the late incoming 11:30 AM–4:36 PM and around the morning low at 9:40 AM.
3. Snook — continuing their fall shift toward back-bay areas, residential canals, creeks and river mouths, with fish also around docks and bridges in the ICW and on shallow flats as the sun warms them. November forecasts note good action around that structure on live sardines, pinfish or shrimp around mangrove points, creek mouths and canal mouths — fish the late incoming 12:00–4:36 PM on the points, then work the backwaters as the weak evening outgoing starts. Check current FWC seasons and slot before keeping one.
Note: conditions are typical for the season today for mid-November — overcast, light south-southwest wind and a high near 80°F in today's forecasts, with cooling water improving the inshore bite in recent reports. Mangrove snapper remain around pilings and rock structure, sheepshead are building around the Skyway pilings, bridge pilings and reef structure on small live shrimp or fiddler crab, and Spanish mackerel remain possible around the passes and just off the beaches while bait schools hold. Nearshore, recent reports note hogfish feeding better over low-relief bottom as temperatures fall.

Tide windows: high 1:02 AM (3.05 ft), low 9:40 AM (-0.15 ft), high 4:36 PM (1.91 ft) and low 7:29 PM (1.76 ft) at station 8726674 — a falling tide to a very low morning low for creek mouths and potholes, then a long incoming through mid-afternoon for flooded mangroves and grass flats, then a weak outgoing to early evening.
Bait: live sardines / whitebait (redfish and snook) + live shrimp (trout, snook and sheepshead), with pinfish, fresh cut bait, gold spoons and soft-plastic jigs as backups. Find a bait shop near the ramp · Check today's tides & forecast.
Compiled from Hubbard's Marina, Captain Experiences guide reports, Tampa Bay Fishin' Report & local tackle shops — general areas only, no secret spots burned. Curated roundup from public sources and seasonal patterns.

October

What's Biting Now

• King mackerel — the fall run is on! Kings migrating south past the bay
• Redfish — big schools on the flats, bulls near the passes
• Snook — harvest open until Nov 30, then closed Dec–Feb
• Spotted seatrout — bite improving as water cools
• Spanish mackerel & pompano — arriving inshore

Old Salt Fall King of the Beach — Nov 12–14, Madeira Beach. 500+ teams, $300K+ in prizes.
Don't forget

Licenses & Seasons

• FL saltwater fishing license required — get one at GoOutdoorsFlorida.com
• Snook season (Gulf): open Mar–Apr & Sep–Nov; closed Dec–Feb & May–Aug
• Measure fish pinched tail, lying flat — when in doubt, let it go
• Regulations change — always verify with FWC before keeping fish

Tap a fish to jump to its picture, size and limit.

Snook

SLOT 28–33 inKeep 1Open Mar–Apr and Sep–Nov

How you know: Thick black line running down its side, pointy snout, and the lower jaw pokes out in front.

You also need the snook permit added to your license to keep one.

Redfish

SLOT 18–27 inKeep 1Max 2 per boat

How you know: Copper-red back and a black spot (sometimes two) right at the base of the tail.

No spot at the tail? Look again before you keep it.

Spotted Seatrout

SLOT 15–19 inKeep 31 over 19 in per boat is OK

How you know: Soft gray-green body covered in black spots — the spots cover the tail fin too.

Tarpon

CATCH AND RELEASEKeep 0

How you know: Giant silver scales like armor and a huge mouth that points up.

Keeping one needs a $50 FWC tag and is only allowed for a record try. Over 40 inches, it stays in the water while you unhook it.

Spanish Mackerel

Min 12 in (fork)Keep 15

How you know: Silver torpedo with yellow spots and a yellow tail fin.

Measured to the fork of the tail.

King Mackerel

Min 24 in (fork)Keep 3

How you know: A long silver missile. Grown kings have no spots, and the dark line down the side dips down sharply in the middle.

Measured to the fork of the tail.

Cobia

Min 36 in (fork)Keep 1Max 2 per boat

How you know: Brown with a wide, flat head like a shark and a dark stripe through the eye.

Look for them under rays, buoys and floating stuff.

Tripletail

Min 18 inKeep 2

How you know: Looks like a big floating leaf — the fins line up so it seems to have three tails.

Hangs under buoys, crab-trap floats and markers, floating on its side.

Mangrove Snapper

Min 10 inKeep 5

How you know: Gray-brown snapper with a dark stripe running through the eye.

Lives around docks, bridges and mangroves.

Lane Snapper

Min 10 inKeep 20

How you know: Pinkish with yellow stripes and one black spot on its side.

Sheepshead

Min 12 inKeep 8

How you know: Black and silver stripes like a jail uniform — and flat teeth that look like a person's.

Eats shrimp and fiddler crabs off dock and bridge pilings.

Flounder

Min 14 inKeep 5CLOSED Oct 15 – Nov 30

How you know: Flat as a pancake with BOTH eyes on top. Brown on top, white underneath.

Lies flat on the sand and ambushes bait.

Red Grouper

Min 20 inKeep 2

How you know: Reddish-brown with pale blotches and a squared-off tail.

All grouper kinds together: max 4 per day.

Gag Grouper

Min 24 inKeep 2Short season — check FWC

How you know: Gray with dark worm-like markings across the back.

All grouper kinds together: max 4 per day.

Red Snapper

Min 16 inKeep 2Special season — check FWC

How you know: All red-pink, with a pointy snout and red eyes.

The season is short and set each year — check FWC before any offshore trip.

Greater Amberjack

Min 34 in (fork)Keep 1Season — check FWC

How you know: Dark stripe through the eye and a torpedo body built for fighting.

Fights harder than almost anything out here. Measured to the fork of the tail.

Sizes and limits from FWC (July 2026), Tampa Bay / Gulf state waters. Rules change — when in doubt, check MyFWC.com before you keep a fish. How to measure: total length = nose to tail tip with the tail squeezed together. Fork length = nose to the V in the tail. Fish pictures: one matched catalog set, drawn for Boaters Nation.

Rods

Two Rods Cover Saltwater

The bay rod: a 7 ft medium-power spinning combo, 2500–3000 reel, 10–15 lb braid with a 20 lb fluorocarbon leader. This one rod handles redfish, trout, snook and snapper.

Offshore: a 7 ft medium-heavy spinning rod (4000–6000 reel, 30–50 lb braid) for kings and cobia, plus a 6.5–7 ft medium-heavy boat rod for dropping on grouper and snapper. First time offshore? A party boat rents you the rod, supplies the bait and knows the spots.
Tackle box

What to Throw

• Live shrimp — the universal Tampa Bay bait; everything eats it
• Greenbacks (whitebait) — the local candy for snook, trout & reds
• Topwater plugs — dawn patrol over the flats
• Soft plastics on jig heads — paddle tails in new penny & white
• Cut ladyfish or mullet — for bull reds

Grab bait on the way: see the bait shop directory
Timing

⏰ When to Go

• Fish the moving tide — incoming and outgoing beat slack water every time. Check today's tides above
• Dawn & dusk — low light means topwater plugs and aggressive reds, snook & trout
• Night dock lights — snook and trout stack up under lit docks; quiet approach, live shrimp
• Summer: go early — bite dies by mid-morning heat. Winter: wait for the afternoon warm-up
• After a front — falling barometer ahead of storms often triggers a hot bite
Tampa Bay area

Where to Try

• Weedon Island flats — redfish & trout on the grass flats
• Skyway bridge pilings — mangrove snapper, grouper, tarpon (seasonal)
• Fort De Soto — beaches, piers & backwater; great for families
• Egmont Key — run offshore of the island for kings, cobia & tarpon
• Alafia River mouth — snook & reds around the mangroves
• Upper bay creeks — trout & flounder in the potholes
Beyond the bay

Heading Offshore

• Nearshore reefs & ledges (3–9 mi) — king mackerel, Spanish, cobia & tripletail around structure; great on calm days
• Hard bottom & ledges (60–120 ft) — red grouper, mangrove snapper & lane snapper on live pinfish or cut bait
• Deeper drops (120 ft+) — gag grouper, red snapper (seasonal) & amberjack; anchor up-current and chum

Before you go:
• Check the marine forecast — see today's conditions. If seas are 3–5 ft, stay home
• File a float plan — tell someone where you're going and when you'll be back
• 1/3 fuel rule — 1/3 out, 1/3 back, 1/3 reserve. No exceptions
• VHF radio + EPIRB/PLB — cell signal dies fast offshore. See the safety section
• Federal waters start at 9 nm — different bag limits & seasons apply beyond the line. Verify with FWC before keeping fish

Tap a knot to jump to its picture and the steps.

Knot 1 · To a hook

Palomar Knot — the easy strong one

Best for: hooks and lures — the strongest easy knot there is.

1. Fold the line in half so you have a loop.
2. Push the loop through the hook's eye.
3. Tie a simple overhand knot with the loop — don't pull it tight yet.
4. Drop the hook through the loop, wet the line, pull tight. Snip the extra.
Knot 2 · To a hook

Improved Clinch Knot — the classic

Best for: hooks and swivels — the classic everyone learns first.

1. Push the line through the hook's eye, leaving a hand-length of extra line.
2. Wrap the extra end around the main line 5 times.
3. Push the end through the little loop by the eye, then through the big loop you just made.
4. Wet it, pull tight slowly, snip the extra.
Knot 3 · To a hook

Uni Knot — the one that does everything

Best for: almost anything — hooks, swivels, even joining two lines.

1. Push the line through the eye and fold it back so the line doubles up.
2. Make a loop with the extra end, held against the doubled line.
3. Wrap the end through the loop and around both lines 4 to 6 times.
4. Wet it, pull the end to snug the wraps, then slide the knot down to the eye and pull the main line tight.
Knot 4 · To a hook

Trilene Knot — through the eye twice

Best for: hooks and swivels — extra strong, because the line goes through the eye twice.

1. Push the line through the hook’s eye TWICE, so it makes a double loop at the eye.
2. Wrap the loose end around the main line 5 to 6 times.
3. Push the end back through the double loop at the eye.
4. Wet it, pull tight slowly, snip the extra.
Knot 5 · To a hook

San Diego Jam — the strong one

Best for: big hooks and heavy lures — one of the strongest hook knots there is.

1. Push the line through the eye and bring the end back so it lies alongside the main line.
2. Wrap the end around BOTH lines 5 to 7 times, working up away from the hook.
3. Push the end through the little gap by the eye, then through the loop the wraps made.
4. Wet it, pull tight slowly, snip the extra.
Knot 6 · To a hook

Snell Knot — made for circle hooks

Best for: circle hooks — it pulls dead straight, so the hook sets in the corner of the mouth like it should.

1. Push the line through the eye and back through it again, leaving a long loop lying along the hook’s shank.
2. Hold the loop against the shank and wrap it around the shank and the line 5 to 7 times, working down the shank.
3. Hold the wraps in place and pull the main line slowly — the wraps snug down tight on the shank.
4. Pull it fully tight and snip the extra.
Knot 7 · For lures

Non-Slip Loop Knot — lets lures swim

Best for: lures — the open loop lets a lure swim and dart like it’s alive.

1. Tie a simple overhand knot in the line a few inches from the end — leave it loose.
2. Push the end through the lure’s eye, then back through the loose overhand knot.
3. Wrap the end around the main line 3 to 4 times.
4. Push the end through the overhand knot one more time, wet it, and pull the main line tight — leave a small loop at the lure.
Knot 8 · Line to line

Double Uni Knot — line to line

Best for: joining two lines — main line to leader, or braid to leader.

1. Lay the two lines side by side, overlapping by about a hand’s length.
2. With one loose end, form a loop and wrap it around BOTH lines 4 to 5 times, then pull that knot snug (not fully tight).
3. Do the exact same knot with the other loose end, facing the other way.
4. Wet both knots, then pull the two main lines apart — the knots slide together and lock. Snip the loose ends close.
Knot 9 · Line to line

Blood Knot — the slim join

Best for: joining two lines of about the same thickness — smooth and slim.

1. Cross the two lines so they overlap by about a hand’s length, like an X.
2. Wrap one loose end around the other line 5 times, then poke it back through the gap in the middle.
3. Wrap the other loose end around the first line 5 times the other way, and poke it through the same middle gap from the opposite side.
4. Wet it and pull both main lines slowly — the wraps stack up neatly. Snip the loose ends close.
Knot 10 · To the reel

Arbor Knot — line to reel

Best for: tying fresh line onto a reel spool so it doesn’t spin.

1. Wrap the line once around the spool and tie a simple overhand knot around the main line. Snip that extra close.
2. Tie a second overhand knot in the loose end itself — it acts as a stopper.
3. Pull the main line so both knots slide down and snug against the spool.
4. Start winding the reel — the line grips the spool and loads up tight.

Tap a hook or lure to jump to its picture and what it’s for.

Hooks itself

Circle Hook

Best for live & cut bait. The point curves back toward the shank. The fish hooks itself in the corner of the mouth. Do NOT yank — just start reeling.

⚖️ The reef rule: fishing for snapper or grouper with real bait? The law says you must use circle hooks — and they release fish safer too.
The classic

J Hook

Best for lures & trolling. The classic shape. When the fish bites, you lift the rod to set the hook.
Hook + weight in one

Jig Heads

A jig is a hook with the weight already molded on. Thread a soft plastic tail onto it, cast it out, and hop it back along the bottom. Inshore and in lakes, 1/8 to 1/4 oz covers most fishing.
Lure

Gold Spoon

A chunk of curved, shiny metal that wobbles like a hurt baitfish. Cast it out and reel it back steady — Spanish mackerel, trout and redfish jump on it.
Lure

Topwater Plug

Floats on the surface. Twitch the rod tip and walk it side to side — “walk the dog.” Best at sunrise and sunset, and the strike explodes on top where you can see it.
Lure

Soft Plastic Shrimp

Thread it on a jig head, cast it out, let it sink, then hop it slowly along the bottom. It looks like a shrimp getting away — and everything in the bay eats shrimp.
Rig

Popping Cork

A float that pops and clicks on the surface, with a shrimp or small bait hanging under it on a short leader. The noise sounds like feeding fish — trout and redfish come to look.
Lure

Bucktail Jig

A jig head dressed with hair that pulses as it moves. Hop it along the bottom or swim it back steady — snook, flounder and trout all eat it.
Sizes run backwards

Hook Sizes, In Plain English

• Size 6–8 — tiny hooks for bluegill and small panfish. Big number = small hook.
• 2/0 circle — the bay all-rounder: trout, redfish, snapper.
• 5/0–7/0 — offshore size for grouper and big snapper.
Once the number gets a "/0" it flips: a 5/0 is BIGGER than a 2/0.

Never fished before? Start at Step 1 and go in order. By Step 12 you have caught a fish.

Step 1 · Before you go

Grown-ups need a license

Kids under 16 fish free — no license. Grown-ups need a Florida saltwater fishing license, and fishing without one can get you a ticket. The license card at the top of this page shows how to get one.
Step 2 · Your rod

Start with a simple spinning combo

A spinning rod and reel that come together in one package. Medium size is right for Tampa Bay. Any tackle shop can spool it with line for you. It's the easiest setup there is to learn on.
Step 3 · Tie your hook on

Use the Palomar knot

One knot is all you need to start: the Palomar. It's the strongest easy knot there is.

See the Palomar knot steps →
Step 4 · Add a bobber

Your bite alarm

Clip a bobber onto your line about 2 feet above the hook, with a small split-shot weight pinched on under it. The bobber floats on top. When a fish bites, the bobber goes under. That's your signal.
Step 5 · Bait the hook

Start with shrimp

Thread a small piece of shrimp onto the hook so the point just pokes out the other side. Shrimp is Tampa Bay's #1 beginner bait — almost everything here eats it.
Step 6 · Cast it out

Smooth, not hard

Point the rod where you want the bait to land. Swing it forward in one smooth motion and let the line fly off. Whipping it hard just tangles it. Smooth beats strong.
Step 7 · Wait and watch

Watch the bobber

Let the bait sit. Little bounces mean little fish are nibbling. When the bobber goes all the way under and stays under — that's a real bite. Get ready.
Step 8 · Set the hook

One quick snap

Lift the rod tip up fast — one quick snap of the wrist. That sticks the hook in. Firm, not violent: you're setting a hook, not starting a lawn mower.
Step 9 · Reel it in

Steady wins

Reel in steady and keep the rod tip up. If the fish pulls hard, stop reeling and let it pull for a second, then reel again. Never yank — yanking tears the hook out.
Step 10 · Land your fish

You caught one

Slide a net under the fish, or lift it in one smooth motion. Wet your hands before you touch it — dry hands rub off the slime that protects the fish's skin.
Step 11 · Take the hook out

Pliers make it easy

Hold the fish gently and push the hook out backwards with pliers — the way it went in. If a fish swallowed the hook deep and you're letting it go, cut the line close to the hook instead. The hook rusts away.
Step 12 · Keep it or let it go

Check the size first

Keeping it? Measure it and check the Fish Chart — a fish that's too small has to go back, it's the law. Keepers go straight on ice. Letting it go? Hold it in the water, move it slowly back and forth, and let it swim out of your hands on its own.

See the Fish Chart →

You caught it — now make it dinner. Go slow. A sharp knife does the work for you.

First · The law

Size-limit fish stay whole until you’re home

A fish with a size limit has to stay whole — head, tail and all — until you're back on land. Filleting one on the boat or at the ramp can get you a ticket. Fillet at home.
You need

Your tools

A sharp fillet knife, a cutting board, pliers, a bowl of clean water, zip bags and a cooler of ice. A dull knife means hard work and cut fingers — sharp is safer.
Step 1

Ice it right away

The moment you decide to keep a fish, it goes on ice. A cold fish fillets cleaner and tastes ten times better.
Step 2

Rinse it and lay it flat

Rinse the slime off. Lay the fish flat on the board — right-handed, head pointing left. Keep your holding hand curled, fingers tucked back out of the knife's path.
Step 3

First cut — behind the gill

Cut down right behind the gill plate until the knife touches the backbone. Stop there — don't cut through the backbone.
Step 4

Slide along the backbone

Turn the knife flat, pointing toward the tail. Slide it along the top of the backbone all the way to the tail in long, smooth strokes. Let the bones steer the blade.
Step 5

Take the meat off the skin

Lay the fillet skin-side down. Grab the tail end of the skin with pliers. Hold the skin tight and slide the knife flat between the skin and the meat, cutting away from you.
Step 6

Trim and check for bones

Cut out the dark red strip down the center — that's the strong, fishy taste. Run your fingertips over the fillet: any little bones you feel, pull them out with pliers.
Step 7

Rinse, bag, ice

Rinse the fillet quick, pat it dry, and seal it in a bag. Bury the bag in ice. Eat it within 2 days — or freeze it the day you catch it.
Whole fish instead?

Cleaning a fish whole

Cut the belly open from the tail to the gills and pull the guts out. Cooking it with the skin on? Scrape the scales off with the back of a spoon, tail to head. Rinse inside and out, then ice it.
The 60-second version

How This Works

1. Pick your water — each tab above is a different kind of fishing: Ocean, Bays, Rivers, Lakes (ponds are in the Lakes tab). The fish, the rod and the bait change with the water.

2. One rod covers most of it — a 7 ft medium spinning combo handles the bay, the rivers and most lake fishing. The Gear tab tells you exactly what to buy.

3. Get legal — Florida has TWO licenses: saltwater and freshwater, and you need the one that matches your water. Kids under 16 fish free. Florida residents fishing saltwater from shore get a free shoreline license — but you still have to sign up for it. Fishing from a charter boat? The boat's license covers you. Snook needs a small add-on permit if you plan to keep one.

4. Easiest first fish — a pier or a lake bank, a bobber, a small hook and live shrimp (saltwater) or worms (freshwater). Something WILL bite.

5. Know before you keep — almost every fish here has a size limit, a bag limit or a season. The Fish Chart tab on this page shows every fish with its picture and legal size; FWC's rules at myfwc.com are the final word. When in doubt, let it go.
Freshwater

Lakes & Ponds

What you'll catch: largemouth bass year-round, bluegill everywhere, black crappie ("specks") in the cooler months, channel catfish all day, plus the occasional bowfin and gar.

The lakes: Lake Tarpon (Palm Harbor) is the famous big-bass lake. Also Lake Seminole, Lake Maggiore, Lake Thonotosassa, Lake Carroll, Lake Rogers and Crescent Lake — most have bank fishing and park access, no boat required.

Ponds: neighborhood and retention ponds all over the area hold bass, bluegill and catfish — some of the easiest fishing there is. Public park ponds are fair game; if a pond is posted, gated or behind a community's signs, you need permission. Many park ponds are catch-and-release — read the park sign.

Rod: one 6'6" to 7 ft medium spinning combo, 8–12 lb line. For ponds, a light 6–6.5 ft combo with 6–8 lb line is even more fun.

Bait: live shiners are the #1 Florida bass bait (under a bobber), red worms and crickets for bluegill, small minnows and jigs for crappie, plastic worms and spinnerbaits for lures. Lakes need the freshwater license.

Tap a fish to jump to its picture, size and limit.

Largemouth Bass

No minimum sizeKeep 5Only 1 over 16 in

How you know: Green with a dark stripe down the side and a huge mouth — the corner of the jaw reaches past the eye.

Bluegill

No size limit50 panfish a day

How you know: Small, round panfish with a dark blue flap by its gill and a yellow-orange belly.

The 50 is for ALL panfish kinds mixed together.

Black Crappie

No size limitKeep 25

How you know: Silver with black speckles scattered like a checkerboard.

Best in the cooler months, around docks and brush.

Channel Catfish

No size limitNo bag limit

How you know: Smooth skin with no scales, long whiskers, and a tail with a deep V in it.

Bowfin

No size limitNo bag limit

How you know: One long fin running down its back and a round tail with a black spot.

Strong fighter. The teeth are sharp — use pliers.

Florida Gar

No size limitNo bag limit

How you know: A long, skinny snout full of needle teeth and spotted, armor-hard scales.

Watch the teeth when you unhook it.

Sizes and limits from FWC statewide freshwater rules. Some lakes and Fish Management Areas have their own rules — read the sign at your lake. Fish pictures: one matched catalog set, drawn for Boaters Nation.

Rods & bait

One Rod Covers Freshwater

The lake rod: one 6'6" to 7 ft medium spinning combo with 8–12 lb line. For ponds, a light 6–6.5 ft combo with 6–8 lb line is even more fun.

Bait: live shiners are the #1 Florida bass bait (fished under a bobber), red worms and crickets for bluegill, small minnows and little jigs for crappie, plastic worms and spinnerbaits when you want lures.

The bobber rig: hook, small split shot, bobber clipped a foot or two above the hook. Cast it near weeds, docks or fallen trees and watch the bobber — when it goes under, reel.
What to buy & where

Gear & Bait Shops

Buying a rod, in plain English: length = how far you cast (7 ft is the all-around answer). Power = how stiff it is (medium for lakes and the bay). Buy a rod-and-reel COMBO first — it's matched at the factory and costs less.

Tackle shops on our map: Tampa Fishing Outfitters, St. Pete Fishing Outfitters, Tarpon Fishing Outfitters, Economy Tackle, Dogfish Tackle, Tackle Shack — open the Boater's Map and tap Fishing Tackle. Budget route: Bass Pro Shops Tampa, Walmart, Dick's.

Bait shops: Gandy Bait & Tackle, Skyway Bait and Tackle, Hubbard's Marina, O'Neill's Marina, Ruskin Bait and Tackle — on the map under Bait. Get an aerated "bubble bucket" or your shrimp die before the fish see them.

Circle Hook

Best for live & cut bait. The point curves back toward the shank. The fish hooks itself in the corner of the mouth. Do NOT yank — just start reeling.

J Hook

Jig Heads

Lure

Plastic Worm

A soft worm rigged weedless — the hook point hides in the worm — with a small bullet weight in front. Drag and hop it slowly through weeds and brush, where bass hide.
Lure

Spinnerbait

A wire frame with a spinning blade and a rubber skirt. Just cast and reel steady past stumps and grass — the flash and thump call bass in. The easiest bass lure there is.
Lure

Crappie Jig

A tiny jig head with a small soft tail. Fish it slow around docks, pilings and brush piles — crappie and bluegill can’t leave it alone.

New to Boating

New to boating? The 8 steps below, in the right order. No experience assumed.

1Get legal first

Born on or after Jan 1, 1988? Florida requires a Boating Safety Education ID card to operate a boat with 10 HP or more. Take an approved course and carry the card.

→ 2Gear up: the safety checklist

Life jackets for everyone, throwable cushion, fire extinguisher, flares, horn, kill-switch lanyard. See exactly what the Coast Guard requires.

→ 3Rent before you buy

Try different boats through rentals or a boat club before spending a dollar. Learn what you actually like on the water first.

→ 4Learn the markers

“Red, right, returning” — channel markers, no-wake signs, and who has the right of way. The rules that keep everyone safe.

→ 5Launch, dock & anchor

Ramp etiquette, docking without the drama, knots that hold, and anchoring that actually sticks.

→ 6Respect Tampa Bay

Skinny water outside the channels, strong tidal current, afternoon lightning, and slow-speed manatee zones. Local knowledge that saves props and tickets.

→ 7Before every trip

Check the marine forecast, tell someone your float plan, and monitor VHF channel 16. If the bay looks angry, stay at the dock.

→ 8Act like you've been here before

Boating etiquette — the ramp rules, guest rules, and sandbar manners that keep the regulars friendly and get you invited back.

→
Beginner mistakes that cost money

Running aground on a falling tide · getting caught in an afternoon storm · boating with no tow coverage · buying the wrong boat before ever renting one.

Emergency — Trouble on the water? Start here.

Life-threatening emergency: Call 911

Distress on the water: VHF Channel 16 — say “Mayday” three times, then your boat name, your position, what’s wrong, and how many people are aboard. The Coast Guard monitors Channel 16 around the clock.

U.S. Coast Guard — Sector St. Petersburg, 24-hour command center: 866-881-1392. The sector covers Florida’s west coast, including all of Tampa Bay.

Florida Fish & Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) — boating accidents, dangerous boating and wildlife violations, 24 hours a day: 888-404-3922 (or *FWC / #FWC from a cell phone).

County sheriff marine patrols: the Hillsborough, Pinellas, Pasco, Hernando, Manatee and Sarasota county sheriffs all run marine units on these waters — in an emergency, call 911 and the nearest marine unit is dispatched.

Poison Control: 800-222-1222

Fuel or oil spill: National Response Center 800-424-8802

VHF quick list: 16 distress & hailing · 9 hailing & bridge tenders · 22A Coast Guard working channel · 13 bridge-to-bridge

Sources: U.S. Coast Guard Sector St. Petersburg Command Center page and USCG news releases (atlanticarea.uscg.mil / news.uscg.mil); FWC Wildlife Alert page (myfwc.com). Verified Nov 6, 2026.
